appraisal_events.evidence: J'ai entendu que vous refusiez l'amie de Robert... je crois que vous n'avez rien à regretter, vous savez que c'est une horreur, elle n'a pas l'ombre de talent, et en plus elle est grotesque; the duchesse is heureuse pourtant... de faire savoir qu'elle avait eu la primeur de ses ridicules.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme de Guermantes publicly ratifies her aunt's refusal of Saint-Loup's actress friend and demolishes her before the salon; the narrator reports the verdict while ironizing the duchesse's pleasure at having been first to enjoy the woman's absurdity.

appraisal_events.evidence: Un sourire permanent de bon roi d'Yvetot légèrement pompette... sa tournée débonnaire, fainéante et royale, de satisfaire à l'empressement de tous; Formidablement riche dans un monde où on l'est de moins en moins... il était encore d'une grande beauté... de quelque dieu grec.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duc's entrance stages him as a sovereign whom the whole room presses to greet, formidably rich and still god-like in looks, so his local pre-eminence is unmistakable; the narrator simultaneously undercuts him with the tipsy petty-king smile, the shark-fin hand and the money-man's suffisance.

status_effects.explanation: She is flatly declared a horror, wholly talentless and grotesque, with no voice in the room to answer.
Her refusal by Mme de Villeparisis is endorsed as a good riddance, confirming her exclusion from this salon.
She commands the exchange, delivers the deciding verdict and is queried deferentially by d'Argencourt, though the narrator marks her satisfaction as vanity.
The same passage notes the often difficult relations with her husband and that his successes with women faisaient le malheur de la sienne, placing her at a private disadvantage.
Every guest presses forward for his half-extended hand and he distributes greetings like a king making a tour; his fortune and beauty are stressed as further sources of local ascendancy.
The woman demolished in front of the salon is identified precisely as l'amie de Robert, so the contempt attaches to him by association in his own family's drawing room.

ambiguities: The target of the blame is never named in the passage (l'amie de Robert, cette actrice); she is resolved to Rachel via the reference sheet and the established identification of Saint-Loup's actress mistress, and a different resolution would move the negative effect off Rachel entirely.

The duc's portrait fuses genuine grandeur (royal tour, enormous fortune, Greek-god profile) with steady narratorial mockery (roi d'Yvetot légèrement pompette, the shark-fin hand, the money-man's suffisance), so it is genuinely underdetermined whether the movement is elevation or ironic diminishment; it is read here as elevation of his social standing delivered in an ironizing voice.
